newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders meet to prepare for larger future.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders meet to prepare for larger future.

text.p: The European Union's ability to incorporate a wave of new members from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean will be the focus of attention on Saturday when the bloc's leaders meet for a special summit on the EU's future.

With fears growing that talks on a new treaty to prepare for enlargement are stagnating, the leaders are expected to call for negotiations to move along rapidly and be concluded as planned in the middle of next year.
"We will be looking for a reaffirmation of the timetable and maintaining the level of ambition," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring told reporters on Friday evening.

The leaders are also expected to discuss a wide range of foreign policy issues over dinner on Saturday night, including their frustration over being excluded from the latest Middle East peace moves by the United States.
Italy and France said on Friday they hoped the summit would make clear that the EU wanted to play a role in the process.

But the main issue and purpose of the summit is the treaty talks -- formally called the inter-governmental conference (IGC). They are seen as essential to the bloc's ability to expand, bringing in countries from tiny Malta to Poland.
"Without (a new treaty) there can't be enlargement," Spring said.
To date the talks have homed in on what needs to be done, such as changing EU decision-making procedures and streamlining its institutions, but they have not led to any firm agreements.

Ireland, the current EU president which is chairing the talks, believes this is normal at this stage in a 15-month negotiation. It also says the IGC is on track to present a draft treaty to another Dublin summit in December.
"We are confident that we can meet the timetable for a draft treaty," Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told RTE television.
But others worry that the IGC negotiators have set their sights too low.

"The inter-governmental conference must not be reduced to a routine car maintenance check where necessary reforms are being postponed until the future," Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said in a speech in Stockholm this week.
British Prime Minister John Major is facing a difficult summit, which is only a few days before the annual conference of his increasingly Euro-sceptic Conservative party.
Already the most reluctant EU leader when it comes to further European integration, Major will be under pressure from home not to appear too conciliatory.
But his EU colleagues are also expected to make it clear that their patience with Britain -- which is opposed to many of the IGC proposals supported by the majority -- is not unlimited.
Asked if the British might be difficult, Spring said: "There will be difficulties for a particular country at any time but I believe the EU has the will to push ahead."
